description: We are a beginner-friendly team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, passionate about space, technology, and innovation. We welcome teammates interested in coding, web development, UI/UX, research, and data visualization. No expert skills are required—just curiosity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn. Let's collaborate and build a creative, meaningful solution to a NASA challenge together!
summary: Space Relic Quest: Unlock the Lost Missions is a free, game-inspired website that teaches school students about NASA hardware left behind in space: the Spirit and Opportunity Mars rovers, the Apollo 11 lunar module descent stage on the Moon, and Voyager 1, which is still traveling and shown as a contrast. Each relic has a story page with five short tabs (purpose, journey, discoveries, challenges and legacy), NASA images with credits, and a clear status label: mission complete, left on the Moon, or still traveling. Students can rotate NASA 3D models, tap hotspots on clickable illustrations, rebuild a mission timeline in a game, take a 15-question quiz with a source for every answer, earn badges and download an explorer certificate. A printable 45-minute Teacher kit and a glossary help classrooms. The site needs no account, works on phones and laptops, and lists every source on a Sources page. It is an independent student project and is not endorsed by NASA.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Space Relic Quest turns the story of spacecraft left behind into an interactive lesson for school-age students. It covers four relics: the Spirit and Opportunity Mars rovers (mission complete), the Apollo 11 lunar module descent stage (left on the Moon), and Voyager 1 (still traveling, shown as a contrast). Every status is labeled clearly so students can tell finished missions from active ones.

HOW IT WORKS

- Mission pages: five tabs per relic (Purpose, Journey, Discoveries, Challenges, Legacy) in simple language, with a photo carousel that gives a credit and a source link for every image.

- 3D Lab: NASA 3D models (Mars rover, Apollo lunar module, Voyager probe) that students rotate and zoom, plus simple clickable illustrations with 15 hotspots that explain what each part does.

- A 14-event timeline, a Data Lab with charts (planned vs. actual work time, distance driven), a 5-round timeline game, and a 15-question quiz with an explanation and a source for every answer.

- 7 badges, a progress dashboard and an explorer certificate that students can download or print.

- A printable 45-minute Teacher kit with discussion questions, and a glossary.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The project makes NASA mission history approachable and checkable. Students learn by exploring, playing and testing themselves, and teachers get a ready lesson. There are no accounts: progress stays in the visitor's browser, and visits are counted anonymously. The site works on phones, tablets and laptops, and supports keyboard use and reduced motion.

TOOLS

React, Vite, JavaScript, CSS, Three.js for 3D, hosting and anonymous analytics on Vercel, and a Google Form for feedback.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

We built the site around status: every relic is labeled mission complete, left on the Moon, or still traveling, and Voyager 1 is included as a contrast to the abandoned hardware. Accuracy and credit came first: content was checked against NASA sources, every image has a credit and source link, the clickable 3D illustrations are clearly marked as not official NASA models, and no image is AI-generated. The site does not use NASA logos and says it is not endorsed by NASA.
